metadata.description: A Kubernetes cluster as one orderable deliverable — release and network ranges. It carries no node pools: a pool is a KubernetesNodePool record contained by the cluster, ordered, scaled and retired on its own, and a cluster with its pools is a composition (ruling 072, 2026-09-12). A cluster record may therefore have zero worker pools, as a hosted control plane or an EKS cluster does at creation. A Base Class in its own right (ADR-068): its contract is the Kubernetes API, which every conformant distribution honors, so an order placed here can be realized by any provider offering one. Named for the standard, never for a product — distributions (OpenShift, EKS, k3s, …) are the Type tier beneath it and offerings the Provider tier. `pod_cidr`/`service_cidr` are Kubernetes vocabulary, which is why this left `Compute`: a VM or a bare-metal host cannot honor them. Derived from OSAC's `cluster` fulfillment type (osac-project/fulfillment-service; its inline node sets map to KubernetesNodePool records); target Network.VirtualNetwork is registered; the fleet manager is a Software.Service of service_kind fleet-manager (ADR-043 relationship semantics).

release.description: Platform release, e.g. 1.30 (a Kubernetes minor release) or a distribution's release stream.

network.description: Converted verbatim from the flat cluster spec.

api_url.description: Cluster API server URL once Realized.

relationships.description: Provisioned and managed by a hub — a Software.Service of service_kind fleet-manager (hosted control planes): the hub has lifecycle authority — hosted control planes run inside it. For imported clusters use the depends_on (soft) edge instead. Unnamed per ADR-043.

Imported/adopted into a hub's fleet (OCM ManagedCluster semantics): managed, not contained — strength soft because an imported cluster survives hub loss (degrade-don't-break). Mutually exclusive with the contained_by hub edge per cluster-hub pair; unnamed per ADR-043 — the typed target is the context.

context.purpose: Declares a managed Kubernetes cluster — release and network ranges — as one provisionable intent; its node pools are KubernetesNodePool records contained by it.
context.plain_description: The request for a control plane: which release and what internal network ranges it uses. The nodes come as separate KubernetesNodePool orders contained by the cluster, so a cluster with its pools is a composition of records, never one record. A provider (e.g. hosted control planes behind a management hub) turns this into a running cluster and publishes back the API URL, console URL, and admin access that everything deployed onto the cluster then uses. Namespaces, quotas, node pools, and workloads all hang off a cluster record.
use_when: You need to request a new Kubernetes cluster with a declared release rather than hand-building one; the pools follow as KubernetesNodePool orders.
You need cluster-scoped resources (namespaces, node pools, storage classes) to have a single parent record they cannot outlive.
not_for: A distributed storage cluster (Ceph and kin) — that is Storage.Cluster; this type is the container-orchestration platform.
A group of nodes — that is KubernetesNodePool, always, whether ordered with the cluster or later (ruling 072).
works_with: KubernetesNamespace — the isolation boundaries carved inside the cluster.
KubernetesNodePool — homogeneous slices of the cluster's node capacity.
Network.VirtualNetwork — the network the cluster is realized onto.
Container — the workloads scheduled onto the cluster.

Software.Service (service_kind fleet-manager) — the fleet manager above this cluster: contained_by when hub-provisioned/hosted, depends_on (soft) when imported; a cluster hosting a hub is just its contained_by target
